flock-lrpd.name: Flock Safety Falcon license plate readers
flock-lrpd.count_note: 116 citywide, three more permitted but not yet installed (LRPD's own list, released under FOIA request PDFOIA-2025-4004 in January 2026).
flock-lrpd.what_it_is: A small solar- or mains-powered camera on a slim pole, usually at the roadside facing one direction of travel. It photographs every passing vehicle, reads the plate with OCR, and also records a 'vehicle fingerprint' - make, body type, colour, roof rack, bumper stickers, damage - so a car can be searched for even with no plate read.
flock-lrpd.what_it_captures: Plate number, vehicle description, timestamp, and the camera's location for every vehicle that passes. Not a live-monitored video feed; it is a searchable database of where a car has been.
flock-lrpd.how_to_spot: A slim rectangular head about the size of a shoebox on a narrow pole, often with a small solar panel and a black battery box. It points across the lane rather than down it, and sits much lower than a traffic camera - roughly 8 to 12 feet.
flock-lrpd.retention: Arkansas's Automatic License Plate Reader System Act (A.C.A. 12-12-1801 et seq.) requires a government entity to purge captured plate data after 150 days. The statute binds the agency; the vendor holding the same data is not covered by that clause.
flock-lrpd.who_can_see_it: LRPD officers search the system directly. Flock's network also allows sharing with other agencies: EFF documents cited by the Arkansas Times show LRPD data reaching agencies in other states, including Johnson County, Texas.
flock-lrpd.money: Board of Directors approved the first contract in 2020. Resolution 15,892 (7 Feb 2023) and Resolution 16,055 (18 Jul 2023) added 75 more Falcon readers and renewed the software. Resolution 16,489 (4 Nov 2024) renewed the subscription; it was amended on 18 Feb 2025 to add $77,500, taking that renewal from $284,500 to $362,000. On 21 Oct 2025 the board approved two further one-year terms at $345,000 a year - $690,000 total.
flock-lrpd.procurement_note: The city did not run its own competitive bid. Insight Public Sector was selected through Omnia Partners cooperative contract 23-6692-03, a national purchasing agreement that member governments can buy from directly.
flock-lrpd.one_line: Photographs every passing car and stores where it was seen.

flock-other.name: Flock readers run by other agencies and businesses
flock-other.operator: North Little Rock, Sherwood, Jacksonville, Alexander police; private businesses
flock-other.count_note: At least 39 Arkansas law-enforcement agencies use Flock. Retailers run their own: Home Depot and Lowe's readers appear in the open map data for Pulaski County.
flock-other.what_it_is: The same Falcon hardware as the LRPD program, bought separately. A private business's reader watches its own lot but can feed the same searchable network.
flock-other.what_it_captures: Identical to the LRPD readers - plate, vehicle fingerprint, time, place.
flock-other.how_to_spot: Same slim pole and shoebox head; retail units usually sit at lot entrances rather than on public roads.
flock-other.retention: The 150-day state purge applies to government entities. A private operator's own retention is set by its contract, not by the ALPR statute.
flock-other.who_can_see_it: Each owner controls sharing. Business owners can choose to share with police, which is how a retailer's camera becomes part of an investigation.
flock-other.money: Bought jurisdiction by jurisdiction; North Little Rock's and the retailers' contracts are not in this trail yet. Several Arkansas cities - Cabot, Pea Ridge, Mayflower, Greers Ferry, Searcy - suspended or removed their Flock cameras during 2026.

sources.label: KATV - Arkansas cities suspending Flock cameras

flock-other.one_line: The same readers, bought separately by other agencies and shops.

flock-unattributed.name: Flock readers with no operator recorded
flock-unattributed.operator: Not recorded in the open data
flock-unattributed.count_note: The largest single group on this map. A volunteer mapping a camera records what is visible from the street - the make is stamped on the housing, the owner is not.
flock-unattributed.what_it_is: Physically identical to the readers above. The gap is in the record, not the hardware: nobody has attached an owner to these particular poles in the open data.
flock-unattributed.what_it_captures: Plate, vehicle description, time and place, like every other Falcon.
flock-unattributed.how_to_spot: Same slim pole and shoebox head.
flock-unattributed.retention: Depends who owns it - 150 days if a government entity, contract terms if a business.
flock-unattributed.who_can_see_it: Unknown, which is the point of the category.
flock-unattributed.money: Untraced. Matching these against LRPD's own 116-camera list, released under FOIA, is the obvious way to close the gap.
flock-unattributed.one_line: Mapped readers whose owner nobody has recorded.

other-camera.name: Other mapped cameras
other-camera.what_it_is: Surveillance cameras recorded in OpenStreetMap that are not plate readers or acoustic sensors.
other-camera.what_it_captures: Video, scope depending on the owner.
other-camera.one_line: Mapped cameras that are not readers or sensors.

other-alpr.name: Non-Flock plate readers
other-alpr.vendor: Genetec, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Leonardo (ELSAG), LiveView Technologies
other-alpr.what_it_is: Plate readers from Flock's competitors. Motorola's Vigilant and Leonardo's ELSAG units are the older style, often mounted on poles at intersections or on patrol cars. LiveView Technologies units are the trailer-mounted camera towers seen in big-box parking lots.
other-alpr.what_it_captures: Plate reads and timestamps; the mobile versions capture wherever the vehicle drives.
other-alpr.how_to_spot: ELSAG and Vigilant heads are squat cylinders or wedge boxes in pairs, angled at the lanes. LVT towers are unmistakable - a trailer with a mast, floodlights and solar panels.
other-alpr.retention: Government operators are covered by the same 150-day purge.
other-alpr.money: Not yet traced in this trail.
other-alpr.one_line: Plate readers from Flock's competitors, including car-mounted ones.

shotspotter.name: ShotSpotter / SoundThinking gunshot detection
shotspotter.count_note: Sensor positions are not published. The map shows the handful volunteers have spotted; a real deployment uses far more, roughly 20-25 microphones per square mile.
shotspotter.what_it_is: Acoustic sensors on rooftops and poles that listen continuously for impulsive sounds. When several hear the same bang, the system triangulates the position, a human reviewer at the vendor classifies it, and an alert with coordinates goes to dispatch - usually inside a minute.
shotspotter.what_it_captures: Loud impulsive sounds and their location. The sensors buffer audio around a detection, which is how a recorded voice has surfaced as evidence in other cities - the reason critics treat 'it only records gunshots' as too simple a claim.
shotspotter.how_to_spot: Hard to spot deliberately. A weatherproof box, often on a tall building parapet or utility pole, with a small microphone port and no lens.
shotspotter.retention: Set by contract with the vendor rather than by the ALPR statute.
shotspotter.who_can_see_it: Alerts go to LRPD dispatch and the Real Time Crime Center.
shotspotter.money: First bought June 2018 - a two-year contract worth $290,000, paid with a US Department of Justice grant. Renewed February 2021 for $287,393. The city later moved it onto local money: a fourth amendment in February 2025 for $188,000 from account 105201-61350, and a further renewal in February 2026. Board votes have been close and repeatedly contested.

sources.label: Arkansas Times - board renews gunshot surveillance

shotspotter.one_line: Microphones that listen for gunfire and triangulate it.
shotspotter.not_mapped_because: An array needs roughly 20 to 25 microphones per square mile to triangulate, over a coverage area that started at two square miles. The few pins here are the ones volunteers spotted; the real layout is not public.

rtcc-lrpd.name: LRPD Real Time Crime Center cameras
rtcc-lrpd.vendor: Flock Safety via Insight Public Sector
rtcc-lrpd.count_note: 75 cameras approved in February 2023 for about $215,800. Individual positions are not published.
rtcc-lrpd.what_it_is: A staffed room where live camera feeds, plate reader hits and gunshot alerts are watched together and pushed to officers on the street. It runs on Axon's Fusus platform, which joins those separate systems into one searchable console and adds object recognition, so an operator can search footage for a described vehicle rather than watch it.
rtcc-lrpd.what_it_captures: Live video that can be watched and recorded, alongside the ALPR and gunshot feeds.
rtcc-lrpd.how_to_spot: Usually a dome or bullet camera cluster on a city pole, sometimes with a blue-lit box, at intersections and in parks.
rtcc-lrpd.retention: Video retention is set by department policy rather than by the ALPR statute.
rtcc-lrpd.who_can_see_it: LRPD staff in the centre, and officers it dispatches information to.
rtcc-lrpd.money: Resolution 15,892 (7 Feb 2023) approved 75 cameras at roughly $215,800. The subscriptions that keep them running come through the same Insight Public Sector contract as the plate readers - the February 2025 amendment added $77,500 for the centre from account 105225-63360.
rtcc-lrpd.one_line: Live camera feeds watched in one staffed room.
rtcc-lrpd.not_mapped_because: 75 cameras were approved in February 2023 for about $215,800 and the subscriptions still appear in the budget, but the department has never published where they are.

ardot-cctv.name: ARDOT traffic cameras
ardot-cctv.operator: Arkansas Department of Transportation, Traffic Management Center
ardot-cctv.count_note: 554 camera feeds are published statewide on IDriveArkansas; 178 of them are in this county. ARDOT's own ITS page describes 'almost 440 department-owned pan-tilt-zoom traffic cameras' plus 100 dynamic message signs and a dozen highway advisory radio sites.
ardot-cctv.what_it_is: Pan-tilt-zoom cameras on tall masts along the interstates, watched around the clock from ARDOT's Traffic Management Center so operators can see crashes, debris and congestion and set the message signs accordingly.
ardot-cctv.what_it_captures: Live video. ARDOT publishes most of these feeds to the public - the map links straight to each camera's stream. They are not plate readers, though a PTZ camera zoomed in can read a plate.
ardot-cctv.how_to_spot: A dome or a long bullet housing at the top of a mast 30 feet or higher, usually with a white cabinet at the base. Models in the published inventory include the Axis P5635-E Mk II, P5655-E and Q6215-LE.
ardot-cctv.retention: Published as live streams; ARDOT does not publish a retention schedule for recorded footage.
ardot-cctv.who_can_see_it: Anyone - the feeds are on IDriveArkansas.com.
ardot-cctv.money: Funded through ARDOT's ITS programme rather than a single city vote.

sources.label: IDriveArkansas camera feed (the layer this map reads)

ardot-cctv.one_line: State traffic cameras - and you can watch these yourself.

ardot-wwd.name: ARDOT wrong-way detection
ardot-wwd.count_note: About 155 sensor sites statewide when complete. Little Rock was the first city to get them, in 2024; installation has since moved along I-40 towards Memphis and onto I-55.
ardot-wwd.what_it_is: Equipment at freeway ramps that detects a car entering against traffic. ARDOT's own description of a site lists 'vehicle sensors, closed-circuit television cameras, illuminators, hardware controllers, warning devices, and communications equipment'. Radar and infrared sensors do the detecting; LED signs flash at the driver; an alarm goes to the Traffic Management Center, which can alert state police.
ardot-wwd.what_it_captures: Vehicle presence and direction, plus camera views of the ramp. This is the important part for anyone comparing the map to IDriveArkansas: the cameras in these kits are part of the safety system and are not published as public traffic feeds.
ardot-wwd.how_to_spot: Look at ramps, not the mainline. A short pole near the ramp terminal carrying one or two small heads, a separate radar-looking panel, sometimes a floodlight-shaped illuminator, a cabinet at the base, and red WRONG WAY signs with LED borders nearby. The concrete pads and pull boxes often appear in Street View a year or more before the equipment does.
ardot-wwd.who_can_see_it: ARDOT's Traffic Management Center; the video is not on the public map.
ardot-wwd.money: ARDOT has described the statewide programme as costing just under $55 million to install, test and maintain.

sources.label: ARDOT NR 25-204 - ramp closures to test the systems
Roads & Bridges - Arkansas testing wrong-way detection

ardot-wwd.one_line: Ramp sensors and cameras that catch wrong-way drivers.
ardot-wwd.not_mapped_because: ARDOT's own component list for a wrong-way site includes cameras and illuminators, and those cameras are not published as public traffic feeds. Only the ramps where equipment has been seen can be shown.

ardot-managed-lane.name: I-430 bridge managed lane
ardot-managed-lane.operator: Arkansas Department of Transportation, Traffic Management Center
ardot-managed-lane.count_note: One corridor: the Arkansas River bridge on I-430 and its approaches.
ardot-managed-lane.what_it_is: Arkansas's first managed lane. The outside shoulder opens as a fourth running lane at peak times and closes the rest of the day. Overhead gantries show a green arrow or a red X above the lane, and the corridor is instrumented so the Traffic Management Center can see the lane is clear before opening it.
ardot-managed-lane.what_it_captures: Traffic video used to check the lane for stalled cars and debris. The red X and green arrow signals themselves are signs, not sensors.
ardot-managed-lane.how_to_spot: Overhead mast arms across the carriageway carrying a lane-control signal per lane, with small cameras and detector heads on the same arm. Between the bridge and I-40 the poles repeat every few hundred metres.
ardot-managed-lane.who_can_see_it: ARDOT's Traffic Management Center, staffed 24/7. A few of the corridor's cameras are on the public map; most of the detection gear is not.
ardot-managed-lane.money: ARDOT has said building the managed lane rather than a new bridge saved more than $240 million. It opened to traffic in March 2023.

sources.label: ARDOT - I-430 bridge managed lane now operational

ardot-managed-lane.one_line: Gantries that open the I-430 shoulder at rush hour.

small-cell.name: Small cell / carrier antennas
small-cell.what_it_is: A short-range mobile base station - the tall smooth canister on top of a slim pole, or a cylinder bolted to a utility pole arm with a cabinet below. They add capacity where phone traffic is dense.
small-cell.what_it_captures: Nothing visual. It is a radio, not a camera. A carrier's network necessarily knows which phones connect to which cell, which is a privacy question of a different kind, but this is not a device that watches the street.
small-cell.how_to_spot: A featureless cylinder with no lens and no glass, usually on top of the pole, with a fat cable running down and a metal cabinet at the base. Included here because it is the single most common thing mistaken for a surveillance camera.
small-cell.money: Private infrastructure, permitted through the city right-of-way process rather than bought with public money.
small-cell.one_line: A phone mast, not a camera. The usual false alarm.

drones.name: Police drones
drones.operator: Little Rock and North Little Rock police departments
drones.one_line: Aircraft that bring a camera anywhere, with no fixed location to map.
drones.what_it_is: Both departments fly drones, and both won state grants in April 2025 to widen the programme. LRPD's launched with eight certified operators. Nationally the model is moving towards drone-as-first-responder, where a drone launches on a 911 call and arrives before officers do.
drones.what_it_captures: Live and recorded video from above, including over private property it flies across on the way. DFR platforms elsewhere carry thermal sensors, plate readers and 3D mapping.
drones.how_to_spot: You mostly do not. A quadcopter at altitude is a dot; the sound arrives late.
drones.who_can_see_it: The flight crew and, where the feed is integrated, the real time crime centre.
drones.money: State grants awarded to both departments in April 2025.
drones.not_mapped_because: It moves. There is no pole to put a pin in - the coverage area is wherever it was flown that day.

fusus.name: Axon Fusus - the software behind the crime centre
fusus.one_line: The layer that joins every other device on this page into one screen.
fusus.what_it_is: Not a device - the platform the Real Time Crime Center runs on. It pulls cameras, plate reader hits, gunshot alerts and drone feeds into a single console, and adds object recognition on top so an operator can search video for a described vehicle or person rather than watch it.
fusus.what_it_captures: Nothing by itself. Its significance is that it makes separate systems searchable together, which is a different capability from any one of them.
fusus.how_to_spot: Invisible. The only outward sign is a registry sticker in a shop window where a business has connected its own cameras.
fusus.money: Bought as part of the Real Time Crime Center programme.
fusus.not_mapped_because: It is software. Its footprint is every camera it is connected to, including private ones whose owners opted in.

facial-recognition.name: Facial recognition
facial-recognition.one_line: Policy exists; use is restricted to specific felony investigations.
facial-recognition.what_it_is: Matching a face in an image against a database of known faces. LRPD documents show a policy permitting it in specific felony investigations with the written approval of the Chief of Police, after the department had previously said it did not use the technology.
facial-recognition.what_it_captures: Identity, from any image good enough to work with - including footage from cameras installed for another purpose.
facial-recognition.how_to_spot: Nothing to spot. It is applied to images after the fact.
facial-recognition.who_can_see_it: Investigators, under the approval process in the policy.
facial-recognition.not_mapped_because: It is a capability applied to footage, not a box on a pole. Any camera on this map is a potential input.

sources.label: Little Rock police facial recognition policy

presence-analytics.name: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth presence analytics
presence-analytics.one_line: Ordinary Wi-Fi access points counting the phones that walk past.
presence-analytics.what_it_is: A phone with Wi-Fi or Bluetooth on announces itself constantly, whether or not it joins anything. Access points and BLE beacons log those probes to count visitors, measure dwell time, tell staff from customers, and estimate a position by comparing signal strength across several APs - roughly 2 to 4 metres of accuracy indoors. It is a standard feature of commercial Wi-Fi, not special equipment.
presence-analytics.what_it_captures: A device identifier, signal strength, time, and often an estimated position on a floorplan. If the device joins the network or signs in, the identifier stops being anonymous.
presence-analytics.how_to_spot: You cannot. It is the same ceiling access point that serves the Wi-Fi.
presence-analytics.retention: Whatever the operator sets. Nothing in the platform requires deletion.
presence-analytics.who_can_see_it: Whoever runs the network, plus any analytics vendor they forward the feed to.
presence-analytics.money: Private. Bundled into ordinary network hardware, which is exactly why it spreads without any procurement debate.
presence-analytics.not_mapped_because: Effectively every building with managed Wi-Fi is a potential sensor, and none of it is published anywhere. Mapping it would mean mapping commercial Wi-Fi itself.

travel-time.name: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi travel-time readers
travel-time.one_line: Roadside boxes that match your phone at two points to time the trip.
travel-time.what_it_is: The roadway version of presence analytics. A reader records the identifier a passing phone or car radio broadcasts, a second reader further along records it again, and the difference gives a travel time. Re-identification rates run a few percent of traffic - enough for statistics, and enough to be an identifier trail.
travel-time.what_it_captures: A wireless identifier, a time and a place, twice.
travel-time.how_to_spot: A small featureless box on a pole with no lens, often solar powered, at regular spacing along a corridor.
travel-time.who_can_see_it: The operating agency and its data vendor.
travel-time.not_mapped_because: Listed for completeness, not because it has been confirmed here. The technology is common at state DOTs, but nothing found so far shows ARDOT running it in Pulaski County - and a box with no lens is exactly the kind of thing that gets mistaken for something else.

cv-screening.name: Commercial vehicle screening
cv-screening.one_line: Weigh-in-motion and transponders that identify trucks at highway speed.
cv-screening.what_it_is: Sensors in the pavement weigh a lorry as it drives over, while transponders and plate readers identify the carrier and check its safety record before it reaches the scales. Arkansas piloted weigh-in-motion on I-40 and I-55 from 2017, and PrePass and Drivewyze bypass systems operate at Arkansas stations.
cv-screening.what_it_captures: Vehicle weight, class, plate and carrier identity, with a timestamp. Aimed at commercial vehicles rather than the public.
cv-screening.how_to_spot: Gantries and roadside cabinets on the approach to a weigh station, with sensor strips cut into the road surface.
cv-screening.who_can_see_it: Highway police and the bypass service operators.
cv-screening.not_mapped_because: Site locations are known in general (the weigh stations) but the sensor positions are not published, and the county's stations sit outside this map's window.

lvt-tower.name: Mobile camera towers
lvt-tower.one_line: The solar trailer with a mast and floodlights in the car park.
lvt-tower.what_it_is: A trailer-mounted camera tower, towed into a car park and left there. Cameras, floodlights, speakers and solar panels on a mast, monitored remotely.
lvt-tower.what_it_captures: Video of the car park, often with plate reading and analytics, and a speaker for a remote operator to talk to you.
lvt-tower.how_to_spot: Unmistakable - a trailer with a telescoping mast, solar panels and blue-white floodlights.
lvt-tower.who_can_see_it: The retailer and its monitoring contractor, and police if footage is requested or the feed is shared.

unidentified.name: Not yet identified
unidentified.what_it_is: Something real, photographed at a real place, that this project has not confidently named yet. Each one carries a note on what it probably is and what evidence would settle it.
unidentified.what_it_captures: Unknown - that is the point of listing it.
unidentified.one_line: Photographed, not yet named. Notes say what would settle it.
